question: A recent article by Intelligence Online reported that a security and defence partnership with Australia is in its final stages, under the direct leadership of the President of the Commission and without prior consultation of the European External Action Service (EEAS)1.

However, Article 24(1) of the Treaty on European Union is very clear: the Commission, and, by extension, its President, has no power of initiative or negotiating mandate in the field of the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), which falls under the exclusive competence of the Council, the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, and the EEAS.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Can the Commission explain the reason for this failure to respect institutional balance, the grounds on which these negotiations were launched despite France’s initial veto and why these negotiations were not conducted by the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security, in accordance with the provisions of the Treaties?

In relation to the termination of a major arms contract between France and Australia in September 2021, a decision publicly condemned by Ursula von der Leyen herself2, can the Commission confirm that no discussions are under way to include Australia in the SAFE instrument and that the loss of confidence on the part of a Member State by its very nature rules out any joint armament procurement agreements?

Does the Commission not consider the industrial integration, especially in the field of defence, of non-European countries to run counter to the objective of reinforcing the industrial and technological base of EU defence and European strategic autonomy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.2.2026) The negotiation and conclusion of Security and Defence Partnerships (SDP) follow the arrangements for non-binding instruments.

On 3 December 2025, and in line with the Treaty on European Union1, the Council authorised the High Representative/Vice-President (HR/VP) to launch negotiations with Australia on a possible SDP, which are led by the European External Action Service. The process is still ongoing. On the EU side the SDP will be signed by HR/VP.

An SDP is required for non-exempt third countries to participate in Security Action for Europe (SAFE) joint procurement2. Australian entities can nevertheless participate to a limited extent. SAFE allows up to 35% of a final product’s component cost to originate outside the EU, the European Economic Area/European Free Trade Association or Ukraine. Exceeding this would require a bilateral agreement with the EU.

The launch of negotiations of such a bilateral agreement would be subject to a mandate by the Council. EU defence industrial initiatives aim to strengthen the resilience and capacity of the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base. SAFE therefore fosters investment in the European defence industry to increase production capacity and improve defence equipment availability.
1 Treaty on European Union (consolidated version); OJ C 326, 26 October 2012; https://eur-

lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2012/oj/eng. 2 According to Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 of 27 May 2025 establishing the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) through the Reinforcement of the European Defence Industry Instrument; https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/1106/oj/eng.
